metadata.summary: This UK Delphi consensus addresses the assessment, diagnosis, treatment and surveillance of Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension in children and young people. It covers investigations, ophthalmological assessment, weight management, medical treatment, lumbar puncture and neurosurgical options, with the aim of protecting vision and improving headache. The authors identify areas without consensus, including aspects of medical and neurosurgical management.

target_population: Children and young people with suspected or confirmed Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension
Children with visual impairment or threatened vision associated with suspected or confirmed IIH
Overweight or obese patients with IIH
therapeutic_areas: Medical management with acetazolamide or topiramate

recognition: Check blood urea, electrolytes and bicarbonate in patients taking acetazolamide.

management.severity: Bicarbonate equal to or lower than 18 mmol/L

therapies_index.name: acetazolamide
approved_indications: The Delphi working group recommended considering it as first-line treatment for IIH. This recommendation followed discussion rather than consensus on medical management.
monitoring: Check blood urea, electrolytes and bicarbonate during treatment; correct bicarbonate if its level is equal to or lower than 18 mmol/L.

therapies_index.name: topiramate
approved_indications: Mentioned as a medication used for IIH; 4% of respondents supported it as first-line treatment for patients without visual impairment, without a consensus recommendation.

therapies_index.name: LP
approved_indications: Diagnostic assessment of suspected IIH, unless contraindicated; if acute visual loss accompanies suspected IIH, the first LP should occur within 48 hours when not contraindicated.
Therapeutic reduction of CSF pressure when it is over 28 cmCSF (21 mmHg), to a target of 20-25 cmCSF (15-18 mmHg).
Repeated therapeutic LP should be offered if visual changes worsen and threaten vision during medical management and/or symptoms do not respond to medical management.
therapies_index.administration: Position the patient in the left lateral decubitus position and, if conscious, flex the knees and hips. The maximum number of therapeutic LPs over the course of illness is five; other treatment options should be initiated before that point.
monitoring: Record CSF opening pressure after the fluid stops rising in the manometer; use a transducer if available.
At the first LP for suspected IIH, send CSF for microscopy, glucose and protein. Send an autoimmune screen (aquaporin and MOG antibodies) and/or cytology only when clinically indicated.
Before LP, check clotting in patients with suspected or confirmed IIH only when clinically indicated.

therapies_index.name: weight management
approved_indications: Overweight or obese patients with IIH should be referred to a dietician or weight management team; a dietetic service should be available for patients with IIH.

therapies_index.name: CSF diversion
approved_indications: Described as a surgical option for IIH. Selection of an intervention depends on symptoms, the extent of visual loss and local availability.

therapies_index.name: VPS
approved_indications: Should be considered among emergency neurosurgical options when IIH causes severe grade 4 papilloedema with threatened vision.

therapies_index.name: LPS
approved_indications: Mentioned as a CSF diversion option for IIH; no specific recommendation for its use is given.

therapies_index.name: ONSF
approved_indications: Discussed as a historical emergency intervention to preserve sight in IIH, but not supported by this pediatric consensus.

therapies_index.name: VSS
approved_indications: Should be considered when there is evidence of stenosis of the dominant venous sinus.

therapies_index.name: ICP bolt monitoring
approved_indications: Should be considered for patients with papilloedema and persistently raised opening-pressure measurements on two LPs.

therapies_index.name: GA
approved_indications: Mentioned as an anaesthetic setting for LP, without a recommendation to use it in preference to local anaesthetic.
monitoring: Document the medications used for GA during LP.
For suspected IIH, check end-tidal carbon dioxide during LP under GA and maintain it within the normal reference range at the attending anaesthetist's discretion.

conditions.name: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension
conditions.description: The condition involves elevated CSF pressure without an identified cause. Diagnosis requires assessment for other causes of raised ICP, including structural disease. The modified Dandy criteria and Friedman’s criteria are discussed, but the consensus recommends Friedman’s criteria for diagnosis.
conditions.epidemiology: A UK cohort study reported an incidence of 0.71 per 100,000 at ages 1-16 years, rising with age and weight to 4.18 per 100,000 in obese boys aged 12-15 years and 10.7 per 100,000 in obese girls aged 12-15 years. Other estimates for children range from 0.17 to 1.32 per 100,000 children.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Headache, visual disturbance and papilloedema are typical, while the remaining neurological examination is generally normal. Headache is described as the most frequently reported symptom, with the source giving its frequency as 7599% of cases. Cranial nerve abnormalities, including abducens nerve palsy, may occur. Acute visual loss can threaten vision.

subtypes.name: IIH without papilloedema
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Under Friedman’s criteria, diagnosis remains possible without papilloedema when abducens nerve palsy and criteria B-E are present. The text also describes diagnosis with criteria B-E and at least three of four specified neuroimaging findings.

subtypes.name: probable
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Friedman’s criteria permit a probable diagnosis when criteria A-D and bilateral papilloedema are present despite an LP opening pressure that does not reach the diagnostic threshold.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish the diagnosis using ophthalmological findings, neurological examination, neuroimaging, CSF composition and LP opening pressure.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A definite diagnosis requires papilloedema; a neurological examination normal apart from cranial nerve abnormalities; qualifying neuroimaging; normal CSF composition; and opening pressure ≥280mm CSF in children [250mm CSF if the child is not sedated and not obese] during a properly performed LP. The document also describes diagnostic routes without papilloedema and a probable diagnosis when pressure is not diagnostically elevated.

diagnostic_workup.test: Weight, height, BMI and BMI centile chart
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Document baseline auxology using RCPCH Growth Charts (UK-WHO).

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When clinically indicated in suspected or confirmed IIH.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate suspected raised ICP and exclude hydrocephalus, mass, structural lesions and other causes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Within 24 hours for children with suspected raised ICP accompanied by early morning headache, vomiting, visual disturbance or focal neurological findings; ideally MRI, or CT if MRI is unavailable.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Friedman’s imaging criterion requires normal brain parenchyma without hydrocephalus, mass, structural lesion or abnormal meningeal enhancement.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the brain for findings relevant to diagnosis and for alternative causes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For suspected IIH with normal vision unless contraindicated; MRI is also recommended with MRV within 7 days for suspected IIH.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Friedman’s criteria specify MRI with and without gadolinium for typical patients described as female and obese. Findings discussed in the document include empty sella, posterior globe flattening and abnormalities involving the optic nerves or their sheaths.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate the venous sinuses as part of neuroimaging.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: With MRI within 7 days in suspected IIH; Friedman’s criteria specify MRI with and without gadolinium plus MRV for patients other than the typical group.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Transverse venous sinus stenosis is among the specified imaging findings.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide neuroimaging when MRI cannot be performed.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: If MRI is unavailable or contraindicated under Friedman’s criteria.
In suspected IIH unless contraindicated; the first LP should occur within 48 hours when suspected IIH is accompanied by acute visual loss and there is no contraindication.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Friedman’s diagnostic threshold is ≥280mm CSF in children [250mm CSF if the child is not sedated and not obese]. The consensus states that <20 cmCSF (15 mmHg) indicates normal CSF pressure. Pressure should be read after CSF stops rising in the manometer tube, using a transducer if available.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At the first LP for suspected IIH.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Friedman’s criteria require normal CSF composition.

diagnostic_workup.test: CSF autoimmune screen (aquaporin and MOG antibodies) and/or cytology
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At the first LP for suspected IIH only if clinically indicated.

diagnostic_workup.test: Thyroid function tests, sodium, potassium, creatinine, urea, liver function, calcium, phosphate, magnesium, glucose, vitamin D, and full blood count

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At baseline in children with BMI>25kg/m2.

diagnostic_workup.test: Ophthalmological examination, including visual fields, colour vision, and visual acuity
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In children with suspected IIH; an optician should urgently refer suspected papilloedema to an ophthalmologist.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Papilloedema is a component of Friedman’s criteria. Severe grade 4 papilloedema with threatened vision is identified as requiring consideration of emergency neurosurgical treatment.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Obtain a baseline scan in children undergoing ophthalmological assessment for IIH.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess suitability for LP when clinically warranted.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before LP only if clinically indicated.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Monitor the patient during LP under GA.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During LP under GA in suspected IIH.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The level should be maintained within the normal reference range at the attending anaesthetist’s discretion.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider for 48 hours when opening pressure remains raised on two LPs and papilloedema is present.

follow_up.schedule: After medical treatment for IIH begins, ophthalmological review is recommended 36 monthly, as stated in the document.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with IIH who are overweight or obese.
decision_rules: Refer patients who are overweight or obese for weight management.

recommended_regimens.name: weight management
recommended_regimens.summary: Refer to a dietician or a weight management team; a dietetic service should be available.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document does not specify a paediatric weight-loss target.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with IIH who do not have visual impairment, regardless of BMI.
decision_rules: Consider acetazolamide as initial medical treatment.

recommended_regimens.name: acetazolamide
recommended_regimens.summary: The Delphi working group recommended considering acetazolamide for initial treatment. This recommendation followed its review of respondents’ comments rather than attainment of the prespecified consensus threshold.

response_assessment.method: Ophthalmological review; optical coherence tomography (OCT) is recommended for monitoring.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: There was no consensus on initial medical management. acetazolamide was selected by 46% of respondents, below the consensus threshold; ‘information, general advice, safety netting but no drug treatment for now’ was selected by 18%. The document does not establish the latter response, topiramate or surgery as a recommended alternative for this population.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with IIH and new visual impairment or loss of vision who are taking acetazolamide.
decision_rules: Check blood urea, electrolytes and bicarbonate during acetazolamide treatment.
Correct bicarbonate when its value is equal to or lower than 18 mmol/L.

response_assessment.method: Measure blood urea, electrolytes and bicarbonate.
response_assessment.interpretation: A bicarbonate value equal to or lower than 18 mmol/L calls for correction.

response_assessment.method: Ophthalmological review; optical coherence tomography (OCT) is recommended for monitoring.

supportive_care: Correct bicarbonate when its value is equal to or lower than 18 mmol/L.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Although this guidance appears under new visual impairment or loss of vision, it specifies monitoring for patients already taking acetazolamide rather than recommending its initiation for this population.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with IIH whose vision is threatened by severe grade 4 papilloedema.
decision_rules: Consider an emergency neurosurgical intervention when severe grade 4 papilloedema threatens vision.

recommended_regimens.name: VPS
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider VPS as an emergency neurosurgical option for threatened vision.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: VPS is given as an example of a neurosurgical option; the document does not designate it as the preferred operation.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients whose visual changes progress with a threat to vision despite medical management and/or whose symptoms do not respond to medical management.
decision_rules: Offer repeated therapeutic LP if visual deterioration threatens vision during medical treatment and/or symptoms remain unresponsive.
If CSF pressure is over 28 cmCSF (21 mmHg), lower it to 20-25 cmCSF (15-18 mmHg).
Institute other therapeutic options before the total number of therapeutic LPs reaches five over the course of illness.

recommended_regimens.name: therapeutic LP
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer repeat procedures for progressive, vision-threatening changes during medical treatment and/or symptoms that do not respond to medical treatment; reduce CSF pressure to the specified target when it exceeds the stated threshold.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: A maximum of five therapeutic LPs over the course of illness.

response_assessment.method: Measure CSF pressure; wait until CSF has stopped rising in the manometer tube before taking the reading.
response_assessment.interpretation: If pressure is over 28 cmCSF (21 mmHg), the specified reduction target is 20-25 cmCSF (15-18 mmHg).

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Families should be informed about potential LP complications. The document notes uncertainty about pressure-measurement practice and clinical responses to raised pressure.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with persistently raised LP opening pressure on two LPs and papilloedema.
decision_rules: Consider ICP bolt monitoring when both repeated pressure elevation and papilloedema are present.

recommended_regimens.name: ICP bolt monitoring
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider monitoring ICP in patients meeting both stated findings.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document does not state that medical treatment must fail before this monitoring is considered.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with evidence of stenosis of the dominant venous sinus.
decision_rules: Consider VSS when stenosis of the dominant venous sinus is demonstrated.

recommended_regimens.name: VSS
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider VSS in the presence of dominant venous sinus stenosis.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document does not require prior failure of medical treatment for VSS. It states that paediatric evidence is lacking and that no randomised control trials compare ONSF, CSF diversion and VSS.

special_populations.population: Overweight or obese patients with IIH
special_populations.considerations: Weight management is part of care for this group.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Refer to a dietician or weight management team.

special_populations.population: Patients with IIH without visual impairment
special_populations.considerations: The Delphi survey did not reach consensus on first-line medical treatment. Acetazolamide was the most selected option (46%), irrespective of BMI; the working group subsequently advised considering it as first-line therapy, based on its interpretation of respondents’ comments rather than consensus.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Acetazolamide may be considered as first-line therapy; this recommendation did not arise from Delphi consensus.

special_populations.population: Patients with new visual impairment or loss of vision
special_populations.considerations: For patients taking acetazolamide, blood urea, electrolytes and bicarbonate should be checked. If suspected IIH is accompanied by acute visual loss, the first LP should be performed within 48 hours unless contraindicated.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Correct bicarbonate when it is equal to or lower than 18 mmol/L in patients taking acetazolamide.

special_populations.population: Patients with severe grade 4 papilloedema and threatened vision
special_populations.considerations: The severity of papilloedema and risk to vision warrant emergency intervention.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Consider emergency neurosurgical treatment, such as VPS.

special_populations.considerations: The selected minimum age for diagnosing IIH without prompting MDT discussion was 10 years.
Document the GA medications and check end-tidal carbon dioxide during LP for suspected IIH. The attending anaesthetist determines how to maintain that level within the normal reference range.

artifacts.description: The table uses its first abbreviation–definition pair as the header row.
artifacts.summary: This table defines abbreviations used in the discussion of IIH diagnosis and management.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It helps distinguish diagnostic tests, clinical measures and interventions referred to elsewhere in the document.

artifacts.title: Classical modified Dandy criteria
artifacts.description: The classical modified Dandy criteria suggest checking for all of the following when diagnosing IIH: (1) symptoms attributable to increased ICP; (2) no localising neurological findings apart from unilateral or bilateral sixth nerve palsies; (3) elevated CSF opening pressure despite normal CSF; (4) normal brain imaging without hydrocephalus; and (5) no alternative explanation for raised ICP. The document notes that some authors consider these criteria sufficient.
artifacts.summary: This numbered set presents the classical modified Dandy diagnostic criteria discussed as background to the document’s preferred criteria.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It identifies the findings and exclusions relevant to distinguishing IIH from other causes of raised ICP.

artifacts.title: Friedman’s criteria
artifacts.description: Step 1: Assess criteria A–E for a definite diagnosis of IIH. A requires papilloedema. B requires an otherwise normal neurological examination, allowing cranial nerve abnormalities. C requires normal brain parenchyma, without hydrocephalus, a mass, a structural lesion or abnormal meningeal enhancement: use MRI with and without gadolinium for typical patients (female and obese), and MRI with and without gadolinium plus MRV for others; contrast-enhanced CT may substitute when MRI is unavailable or contraindicated. D requires normal CSF composition. E requires opening pressure ≥280mm CSF in children, or 250mm CSF if the child is not sedated and not obese, measured during a properly performed lumbar puncture. Step 2: Without papilloedema, IIH can still be diagnosed when an abducens nerve palsy accompanies all of B–E. The document also permits diagnosis with B–E plus at least three of these four imaging findings: (i) empty sella, (ii) flattening of the posterior aspect of the globe, (iii) distension of the perioptic subarachnoid space, whether or not the optic nerve is tortuous, and (iv) transverse venous sinus stenosis. Step 3: A probable diagnosis is possible with A–D and bilateral papilloedema even when criterion E does not reach a diagnostic pressure.
artifacts.summary: This structured set distinguishes definite and probable IIH diagnoses and describes the routes specified when papilloedema is absent. The document recommends using Friedman’s criteria for diagnosis.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It links examination, imaging, CSF findings and lumbar puncture pressure to the diagnostic decision while preserving the stated exceptions.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Background: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH) can cause substantial disability. Limited evidence and the absence of national guidance for paediatric diagnosis and treatment have contributed to differing practice. A national Delphi exercise conducted through the Children’s Headache Network (CHaN) sought to develop a practical assessment and treatment pathway. Methods: Experts in the UK considered 104 questions covering assessment, diagnosis, treatment, follow-up and surveillance. Participants were 66 healthcare professionals from general paediatrics, paediatric neurology, ophthalmology, optician practice, neuroradiology and neurosurgery who had an interest in or experience with IIH. Results: The exercise ran from March 2019 to August 2021 and comprised three rounds: Round 1 included 67 questions, Round 2 included 24, and Round 3 (Ophthalmological) included 13. The first two rounds had 54 and 65 responders, respectively. The Royal College of Ophthalmologists endorsed the exercise and engaged 59 ophthalmologists for the third round. Conclusions: The UK consensus offers a pragmatic approach to paediatric IIH. It was endorsed by CHaN and the British Paediatric Neurology Association, and is intended to improve care while reducing both missed diagnoses and overdiagnosis.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: IIH involves raised cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure without an identified cause. Headache, visual disturbance and papilloedema are typical, while the rest of the neurological examination is generally normal. Headache is the most frequently reported symptom, occurring in 7599% of cases as printed in the document. Pseudotumour Cerebri Syndrome (PTCS) is another term that also covers secondary causes. Heinrich Quincke described the condition in the late nineteenth century and attributed it to excessive CSF production. Later names included ‘pseudotumor cerebri’ in 1904 and ‘benign intracranial hypertension’ in 1955; reports of visual loss made the description ‘benign’ inappropriate. Subsequent terminology included PTCS and IIH. The classical modified Dandy criteria suggest that IIH diagnosis requires symptoms of increased intracranial pressure (ICP), no focal neurological signs other than unilateral or bilateral sixth nerve palsies, increased CSF opening pressure with otherwise normal CSF, normal brain imaging without hydrocephalus, and no alternative explanation for raised ICP. Some authors consider these criteria sufficient. Friedman’s criteria provide an alternative. For definite IIH, they require A) papilloedema; B) a normal neurological examination apart from cranial nerve abnormalities; C) normal brain parenchyma without hydrocephalus, a mass, a structural lesion or abnormal meningeal enhancement on MRI with and without gadolinium in typical patients (female and obese), with MRI with and without gadolinium plus MRV for others; if MRI cannot be obtained or is contraindicated, contrast-enhanced CT may be used; D) normal CSF composition; and E) opening pressure of ≥280mm CSF in children, or 250mm CSF if the child is not sedated and not obese, measured during a properly performed lumbar puncture. Without papilloedema, IIH can still be diagnosed under these criteria when abducens nerve palsy and all of B-E are present. The document also describes diagnosis with B-E plus at least three of four imaging features: empty sella, flattening of the posterior globe, enlargement of the perioptic subarachnoid space with or without optic nerve tortuosity, and transverse venous sinus stenosis. A ‘probable’ diagnosis is possible with A-D and bilateral papilloedema when CSF pressure does not meet the diagnostic threshold in E. Diagnosis requires exclusion of underlying structural causes, including malignancy or autoimmune conditions. Potential imaging findings include secondary empty sella syndrome, flattened globes, abnormal optic nerve sheaths, optic nerve protrusion, posterior globe flattening and transverse sinus stenosis. A UK cohort reported IIH incidence of 0.71 per 100,000 among children aged 1-16 years, rising with age and weight to 4.18 per 100,000 in obese boys aged 12-15 years and 10.7 per 100,000 in obese girls of the same age. Other estimates for children range from 0.17 to 1.32 per 100,000. Treatment aims to protect vision and relieve headache. Weight control has been effective in adults. Drug treatment commonly involves acetazolamide or topiramate; a possible weight-loss benefit from topiramate has not yet been established in larger studies. Procedural options include CSF diversion, such as ventriculoperitoneal shunt (VPS) or lumboperitonral shunt, optic nerve sheath fenestration (ONSF), and venous sinus stenting (VSS). Choices depend on symptoms, the extent of visual loss and local availability. Lumbar puncture (LP) has been examined for both diagnosis and treatment, but doubts about its therapeutic efficacy have increased interest in surgery. How best to measure pressure and respond clinically to elevated measurements remains uncertain. With no randomised control trials of paediatric IIH management, this three-round Delphi study examined diagnosis, investigation and management to provide clinicians with recommendations from experienced professionals, following international adult consensus recommendations.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: The study used a Delphi process to examine expert opinion about paediatric IIH in the UK.

document_sections.heading: Study Design Delphi
document_sections.content: An Ovid literature search informed questions concerning paediatric IIH mortality, morbidity, diagnosis, treatment and surveillance. A core group was formed through the British Paediatric Neurology Association (BPNA) Childhood Headache Network (CHaN) specialist interest group. Its 11 experts included paediatric neurologists, paediatricians and ophthalmologists. They reviewed the literature, chose survey questions and consulted patient groups during the work.

document_sections.heading: Delphi consensus method
document_sections.content: The Delphi method was used to generate consensus recommendations. Published methodological guidance cited in the document recommends at least 15-20 expert participants. Agreement thresholds can be as low as 51%, although higher thresholds may be preferable; setting the threshold beforehand can limit bias. This exercise defined consensus in advance as 70% agreement and omitted ‘do not know’ and ‘do not feel qualified to answer’ responses from its analysis. The core group represented paediatric neurology, ophthalmology, neurodisability, community and general paediatrics, neurosurgery, neuroradiology and other areas involved in IIH care. Participants received weekly reminders for three months. Questions were not reused in later rounds; subsequent questions arose from earlier answers. Round one contained 67 questions. The core group then identified matters requiring clarification and formulated 24 refined questions for round two. Previous rounds were not repeated after round two. Round three focused specifically on ophthalmologists because its subject matter concerned their expertise. The Royal College of Ophthalmologists endorsed the exercise, and 13 ophthalmological questions were distributed through its network to UK paediatric ophthalmologists. No invited participant was excluded from a round.

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: The following recommendations arose from topics on which the exercise identified consensus. The document points to Supplementary Table 2 for their summary and Supplementary Table 3 for the full questions and findings.

document_sections.heading: Survey Respondents
document_sections.content: In round one, 114 invitations were emailed and 54 people completed the survey: 33 paediatric neurologists (61%), 5 general paediatricians (9%), 5 neurosurgeons (9%), 4 ophthalmologists (7%), 2 neuroradiologists (4%), one general paediatrician with a special interest in neurology (2%), one optometrist (2%), one community paediatrician (2%) and one patient-group representative (2%). Round two received 65 completed surveys after 127 email invitations. In round three, 59 paediatric ophthalmologists completed the survey.

document_sections.heading: Nomenclature
document_sections.content: The recommended name is ‘Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension’. For possible IIH without red flags, hospital assessment for diagnosis and subsequent management should occur within two weeks. Baseline assessment should include height and weight, with BMI and BMI centile recorded using RCPCH Growth Charts (UK-WHO). Patients with suspected or confirmed IIH should be assessed for obstructive sleep apnoea when clinically indicated.

document_sections.heading: Diagnostic Criteria
document_sections.content: Friedman’s diagnostic criteria should be applied when diagnosing IIH; the document refers to Supplementary Table 1 for those criteria.

document_sections.heading: LP and CSF pressure related to diagnosis of IIH
document_sections.content: For suspected IIH, an LP should be performed to establish the diagnosis unless contraindicated. If suspected IIH is accompanied by acute visual loss, the initial LP should take place ‘within 48 hours’ when there is no contraindication. An opening pressure <20 cmCSF (15 mmHg) indicates normal CSF pressure. A transducer should record CSF pressure when one is available.

document_sections.heading: Neuroimaging
document_sections.content: Children with signs suggesting raised ICP, such as early-morning headache, vomiting, visual disturbance or focal neurological findings, should undergo imaging within 24 hours, preferably MRI or CT if MRI is unavailable. A child with suspected IIH and normal vision should receive brain MRI unless contraindicated. Children with suspected IIH should undergo MRI and MRV within 7 days.

document_sections.heading: MDT meetings for diagnosis of IIH
document_sections.content: Children with IIH features who do not fulfil diagnostic criteria should be discussed by a multidisciplinary team (MDT) including paediatric neurologists, ophthalmologists and neuroradiologists. The selected minimum age at which an IIH diagnosis would not itself trigger MDT discussion was 10 years.

document_sections.heading: Laboratory
document_sections.content: Baseline tests should cover thyroid function, sodium, potassium, creatinine, urea, liver function, calcium, phosphate, magnesium, glucose, vitamin D and full blood count. Children with BMI>25kg/m2 should also have a baseline lipid profile.

document_sections.heading: Ophthalmological assessment
document_sections.content: Baseline B-scan should be performed where available. Opticians should arrange urgent ophthalmologist referral for a child with suspected papilloedema. Children should see an ophthalmologist trained and experienced in paediatric ophthalmology and receive a detailed examination that includes visual fields, colour vision and visual acuity. Baseline optical coherence tomography (OCT) should support diagnosis and monitoring. Once medical treatment for IIH has begun, ophthalmological review should occur ‘36 monthly’, as stated in the document. Severe grade 4 papilloedema that threatens sight warrants consideration of emergency neurosurgical treatment, such as VPS. A regional MDT discussion for suspected paediatric IIH should include paediatricians and/or paediatric neurologists together with ophthalmologists.

document_sections.heading: LP assessment of CSF pressure: Method for LP
document_sections.content: A 10-20 minute online resource teaching LP technique for IIH was considered useful. Families should receive information about possible LP complications. During LP, a conscious patient should have the knees and hips flexed and should lie in the left lateral decubitus position. Clotting tests are unnecessary before LP in suspected or confirmed IIH unless clinically indicated. Pressure should be measured only after CSF has stopped rising in the manometer. At the first LP for suspected IIH, CSF should be sent for microscopy, glucose and protein. An autoimmune screen for aquaporin and MOG antibodies and/or cytology should be requested at that LP only when clinically indicated.

document_sections.heading: LP assessment of CSF pressure with local or general anaesthetic
document_sections.content: Local anaesthetic may be used for LP. When LP takes place under GA, the GA medications should be documented. For suspected IIH, end-tidal carbon dioxide should be checked during LP under GA and maintained within the normal reference range at the attending anaesthetists’ discretion. The document refers to Supplementary Table 4 for the reason for checking it.

document_sections.heading: Management: Therapeutic LP
document_sections.content: If CSF pressure exceeds 28 cmCSF (21 mmHg), it should be lowered to 20-25 cmCSF (15-18 mmHg). A patient should have no more than five therapeutic LPs during the illness because other treatments should be initiated before that limit is reached.

document_sections.heading: Management: Weight management
document_sections.content: Dietetic support for weight management should be available to patients with IIH. Those with IIH who are overweight or obese should be referred to a dietician or a weight-management team.

document_sections.heading: Management: First line therapy in patients with IIH who do not have visual impairment
document_sections.content: No medical-treatment option achieved consensus. The most frequently chosen response, selected by 46% regardless of patient BMI, was to consider acetazolamide as first-line drug treatment for everyone; this fell short of the consensus threshold. After ‘acetazolamide’ (46%) and ‘other’ (26%), the leading choice was information, general advice and safety-netting without immediate medication (18%). Smaller proportions selected topiramate (4%), no intervention (4%) or surgery (2%).

document_sections.heading: Management: First line therapy in patients with new visual impairment / loss of vision
document_sections.content: For a patient receiving acetazolamide, blood urea, electrolytes and bicarbonate should be measured. Bicarbonate should be corrected when its value is equal to or lower than 18 mmol/L.

document_sections.heading: Management: Second line
document_sections.content: Repeated therapeutic LP should be offered if visual changes worsen and sight is threatened despite medical management and/or if symptoms fail to respond to medical management.

document_sections.heading: Management: Neurosurgical
document_sections.content: ICP bolt monitoring for 48 hours should be considered when papilloedema accompanies persistently raised opening-pressure measurements on two LPs. VSS should be considered when stenosis of the dominant venous sinus is demonstrated.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: Across three question rounds, consensus emerged on the timing of initial assessment, body measurements, neuroimaging, eye examinations, some management decisions and the place of a regional MDT. The recommended Friedman’s criteria in Supplementary Table 1 permit diagnosis using clinical findings and neuroimaging criteria.

document_sections.heading: Areas lacking consensus
document_sections.content: Supplementary Table 4 describes unresolved issues: interpretation of CSF pressure measurements, laboratory testing, papilloedema grading, elements of LP technique and neurosurgical care. ONSF did not receive support. Although historically considered an emergency intervention to preserve sight in IIH, its indications in children relative to CSF-diversion approaches such as VPS remain in question. VSS has been used in adults, but randomised control trials comparing ONSF, CSF diversion and VSS do not exist, and paediatric evidence is lacking. Medical management also lacked consensus. Nevertheless, acetazolamide was the most selected first-line medication (46%) irrespective of BMI. After examining comments from respondents who selected ‘other’, including comments about having performed a diagnostic or therapeutic LP and managing weight in parallel, the Delphi working group recommended considering acetazolamide as first-line treatment. This recommendation reflects interpretation of comments rather than consensus and is an exception to the Delphi method’s stated goals.

document_sections.heading: Thematic agreement
document_sections.content: Some response patterns suggested agreement on a theme without resolving the detailed question. Asked when manometer pressure should be read, 38 responses (81%) favoured waiting until CSF stopped rising. In round two, when asked how long to wait after it stopped, 25 responses (50%) favoured reading immediately, 12 responses (24%) selected ‘other’, and 10 responses (20%) favoured waiting ‘after 5 minutes’. On whether high CSF pressure should be reduced until normal pressure is reached, 25 responses (57%) supported doing so and 13 responses (29%) selected ‘other’; only six disagreed. The authors interpreted this as suggesting that 86% favoured lowering high pressure by some amount. For uncertainty in care, they propose discussion by a regional IIH MDT and, where necessary, a national one. They note that MDT discussion may aid diagnostic confirmation, as described previously in the UK.

document_sections.heading: Limitations of survey
document_sections.content: The authors advise future studies to take care with question wording and methods for determining consensus, and to use strategies that increase enrolment and response. Targeted invitations to neurosurgeons could help. Invitations in this survey went to UK professionals experienced in paediatric IIH; this limited pool contributed to variable response rates, particularly for specialised topics. The study did not evaluate response patterns by participant location or the reproducibility of answers. Ambiguous questions lacking context could have changed how participants answered. For example, 27 responses (56.3%) agreed that an LP opening pressure greater than 28 cmCSF should be diagnostic of IIH, but respondents may have answered ‘no’ because raised ICP alone cannot establish the diagnosis or because the 28 cmCSF threshold was presented without context. Although thematic agreement was observed, evaluating it was not a primary objective, so its interpretation was subjective.

document_sections.heading: Conclusion
document_sections.content: The Delphi exercise offers clinicians practical guidance intended to improve care and service delivery for children being investigated for IIH. Supplementary Table 2 organises the recommendations for paediatric management with reference to Friedman’s criteria in Supplementary Table 1; Supplementary Table 3 details the questions and whether consensus was obtained. The survey and recommendations are intended to underpin a nationally endorsed guideline, clinical audit and further research to improve paediatric IIH outcomes. The authors consider the recommendations pragmatic and applicable across most healthcare systems.

document_sections.heading: Availability of data and material
document_sections.content: The corresponding author can provide the study datasets on reasonable request.

document_sections.heading: What is already known on this topic
document_sections.content: The document states that paediatric IIH incidence is rising, that randomised controlled trials on its management are absent, and that management varies with the treating clinician, local or national policy and funding.

document_sections.heading: What this study adds
document_sections.content: The study provides consensus-based recommendations for paediatric IIH management that the authors consider practical to implement in most healthcare systems worldwide.

document_sections.heading: How this study might affect research, practice or policy
document_sections.content: The authors present the new UK guidance for IIH management and surveillance as a consensus basis for delivering clinical care. They also expect its findings to assist policy makers and planners with budgeting and resource allocation for IIH care.
